title: Health-care report highlights chronic conditions, inequities in northern Ontario First Nations
summary: A new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies highlights health-care inequities facing northern Ontario communities, including high rates of rheumatoid arthritis,…

image.caption: Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation, speaks at the Matawa Training and Wellness Centre in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday during the unveiling of Mamow Ahyamowen's latest health-care report. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·New

A new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies highlights health-care inequities facing northern Ontario communities, including high rates of rheumatoid arthritis, chronic pancreatitis and substance use disorder.
61% of band members dying before retirement age, compared to 22% for Ontario overall

Northern Ontario communities have higher rates of early death and chronic disorders compared to the rest of the province, according to a new report by an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies.
The report, called “Reclaiming Our Health: Exploring Chronic Conditions in Participating Northern Ontario First Nations,” was released Thursday in Thunder Bay.
The report focused on 22 chronic conditions among members of 70 First Nations between 2003 and 2022, comparing their prevalance with the provincial average.
It found that for northern Ontario First Nations, rates of rheumatoid arthritis were 14.4 times higher, chronic pancreatitis were 4.7 times higher, and substance use disorder were 4.3 times higher.
Some 61 per cent of band members where dying before retirement age, compared to 22 per cent for Ontario overall.
The data comes as no surprise to Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN), which represents 49 First Nations across Treaties 9 and 5 and was not involved in creating the repport.
“It just reaffirms or validates what we've been hearing from our communities,” said Fiddler.

Maureen Gustafson is the knowledge translation and exchange specialist for Mamow Ahyamowen, an alliance of 11 First Nations health and social service agencies based in northern Ontario. (Marc Doucette/CBC)

But the report offered longitudinal understanding of the health challenges facing northern Ontario communities, said Maureen Gustafson, knowledge translation and exchange specialist for the Mamow Ahyamowen alliance.
“Looking back that far allows us to understand how things have changed over time, looking at trends or patterns,” she said of the report's scope.
Mamow Ahyamowen formed a decade ago with the goal of providing health-care data to First Nations that have historically struggled to obtain this information.
“It's all about giving communities back their data because it belongs to them,” Gustafson said, “but it's often been held by non-Indigenous organizations and institutions.”
Looking back that far allows us to understand how things have changed over time, looking at trends or patterns.Maureen Gustafson, Mamow Ahyamowen
“It's really powerful when the communities can take that back and use it to advance their own goals towards basically self-determination.”
Three of the five most common conditions for community members in 2019 were related to mental health and substance use, the report found:

The report acknowledges that “health administrative data, by definition, relies on people being able to access the health-care system.” The study only includes data from those in both the Indian Register and Registered Persons Database.

Mamow Ahyamowen receives funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health (MOH). Its study was supported by ICES (formerly the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences), which is also funded by an annual grant from the MOH and Ministry of Long-Term Care.
‘They're not just stories; they're real people’
The report documented big increases in some conditions over time, such as cirrhosis, kidney failure, schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders.
However, there were also decreases in rates of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), osteoporosis and congestive heart failure.

A large group of people gathered at the Matawa Training and Wellness Centre in Thunder Bay, Ont., on Thursday to learn about Mamow Ahyamowen's new report, called “Reclaiming Our Health: Exploring Chronic Conditions in Participating Northern Ontario First Nations.” (Marc Doucette/CBC)
“This could mean that fewer community members are being diagnosed with the conditions, but that they aren’t living as long or that more of them are passing away,” the report said.
While the report dealt in statistics, it was important to remember the humans involved, Fiddler said.
“They're not just stories; they're real people,” he said.
“It's important that we honour those people, people like Miranda that lost their lives trying to access the health-care system that she desperately needed to stay alive.”

Miranda Mamakwa died in September at age 31 after she couldn't get to crucial medical appointments following open-heart surgery in April. The member of Fort Severn First Nation leaves three children behind.
Her story featured in a recent CBC documentary about people from northern Ontario First Nations who say they’re being denied access to critical medical care.
When Canada’s health care fails to be ‘universal’

Fiddler said he hopes Mamow Ahyamowen’s report is sent to the provincial and federal governments so that First Nations can “be given resources for them to address the high disease load that they're currently carrying.”
“I look at it as a very powerful planning tool for our communities to use moving forward,” he said.

blocks.text: ‘We need more resources’

The report highlights how health-care partners throughout the region are already at capacity trying to support communities, according to Janet Gordon, vice president of community health for the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, which is part of Mamow Ahyamowen.
“We need more resources. We need the governments to hear us and to understand what the needs are in all of our communities,” Gordon said.
Janet Gordon is vice president of community health for the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, which is part of Mamow Ahyamowen. (Marc Doucette/CBC)
It’s also important to recognize the infrastructure needed to support the delivery of health-care services in remote First Nations, she added.
“There's just that demand for workspace and accommodation at the community level and it's not adequate. Our providers could stay longer if there was space,” Gordon explained.

blocks.text: Mamow Ahyamowen is developing community-specific reports based on the data it’s gathered. After that, it will issue reports on mental health and substance use as well as injuries.

“For us to know that information, it will inform how we deliver services, how we deliver programs, how we can help communities deal with their community-specific priorities in all those areas — mental health, addictions, heart disease, diabetes,” said Gordon.
